strengths: Addresses an important and often overlooked aspect of VR sketch-based 3D modeling: leveraging the temporal sequence of strokes and points rather than treating sketches as unordered point clouds.

Provides a valuable data contribution consisting of both an automated, training-free synthetic sequential sketch generator (producing >20k pairs) and a curated real VR sketch benchmark (900 sketches across 4 categories) with temporal order preserved.

The proposed architecture effectively incorporates dual-level positional embeddings (stroke index and within-stroke point index) with continuous 3D Fourier spatial encodings into a BERT-style encoder and latent diffusion model.
Demonstrates clear and substantial empirical gains over existing baselines (Luo et al. and LAS-Diffusion) on both the established 3DVRChair benchmark and the proposed dataset.

Comprehensive experimental analysis, including zero-shot and few-shot synthetic-to-real transfer, partial sketch completion, and well-designed ablation experiments that validate each design choice (especially the impact of stroke ordering).
weaknesses: The real sketch collection relies on a surface-snapping mechanism onto reference 3D models. While this ensures geometric alignment and clean ground truth, it differs from natural freehand sketching in open 3D space during early-stage ideation, where sketches often exhibit noticeable off-surface drift.

The synthetic sketch ordering relies on a heuristic depth-first traversal of proximity graphs with slight stochasticity. The paper lacks a quantitative or perceptual analysis comparing synthetic stroke sequences against actual human sketching behaviors to verify how faithfully this heuristic approximates human drawing strategies.

The evaluation is restricted to four standard rigid object categories (chairs, tables, cabinets, airplanes) and uses a frozen 64^3 VQ-VAE latent space, which limits fine-grained geometric details and broader cross-category generalization.

strengths: Well-motivated sequential formulation: Treating 3D VR sketches as ordered sequences of strokes and points rather than unordered point clouds or rendered 2D multi-view images is intuitive and effectively captures drawing hierarchy and user intent.

Valuable dataset and synthetic generation pipeline: The paper provides both a heuristic, training-free synthetic stroke generation pipeline (producing over 20k pairs) and a newly collected real VR dataset across four categories (900 pairs) with preserved stroke order, expanding beyond the single-category 3DVRChair benchmark.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The proposed method outperforms existing baselines (e.g., Luo et al. and LAS-Diffusion) by a substantial margin on both 3DVRChair and the proposed dataset across Chamfer Distance and F-score.

Thorough ablation study: The ablation experiments clearly isolate and quantify the impact of each design decision, specifically confirming the tangible benefits of stroke and point ordering, data augmentations, and synthetic pre-training over point-cloud or multi-view representations.

Practical demonstration of partial sketch completion: The paper demonstrates robust shape generation from partially drawn sketches, showing how global structure captured early in the drawing sequence enables interactive design exploration.
weaknesses: Practical applicability of surface-snapping: During real data collection, strokes are projected onto a reference 3D model using a surface-snapping mechanism. While this reduces depth ambiguity, it does not reflect genuine freehand ideation where no ground-truth reference model exists to snap onto, potentially limiting out-of-the-box performance on completely freehand sketches in the wild.

Heuristic stroke ordering: Synthetic stroke ordering is generated via depth-first search on a spatial proximity graph with stochastic skipping, which does not necessarily reflect human semantic drawing behavior (e.g., sketching base/scaffolding parts before secondary features).

Resolution and detail bounded by frozen latent representation: The generator relies on SDFusion with a frozen 64^3 3D VQ-VAE, leading to noticeably oversmoothed predictions and limiting the model's ability to reproduce fine-grained geometric details.

Limited category diversity: Although a marked improvement over prior single-category VR sketch benchmarks, the evaluation is still restricted to four rigid object categories from ShapeNet (chairs, tables, cabinets, airplanes).

strengths: Compelling and intuitive motivation: Unlike previous works that treat 3D VR sketches as unordered point sets, this work explicitly models the temporal hierarchy (stroke order and intra-stroke point order), which naturally reflects the physical design process and structural intent.

Comprehensive data pipeline: The paper provides both an effective, training-free synthetic sketch synthesis pipeline (yielding ~20k pairs) and a newly collected real benchmark across four categories (900 sketches) with a surface-snapping interface that meaningfully reduces depth-perception noise.

Well-adapted architecture: The BERT-style sequential encoder is well tailored for 3D strokes, incorporating spatial Fourier features, discrete delimiter tokens, and continuous sequence position encodings to condition a latent SDF diffusion model (SDFusion).

Thorough experimental validation: The method shows strong improvements over existing baselines (e.g., Luo et al., LAS-diffusion) on both the legacy 3DVRChair dataset and the new benchmark. Ablations clearly isolate the benefits of stroke ordering, sketch augmentations, synthetic pretraining, and sequential vs. point-cloud/multi-view formulations.
Useful application demonstrated: The model demonstrates convincing performance on partial sketch completion, achieving good shape synthesis from as little as 50% of the sketch sequence.
weaknesses: Restricted semantic diversity: The dataset and experiments are confined to four canonical ShapeNet categories (chairs, tables, cabinets, airplanes). It remains unverified how well the method scales to non-rigid or organic geometries (e.g., animals, characters, garments).

Snapping constraint vs. freehand exploration: The real data collection utilizes surface snapping onto existing 3D reference models to ensure alignment. While this creates clean supervision, in practical early-stage VR ideation users sketch in free space without an underlying reference mesh, which might introduce different types of spatial errors not fully captured during collection.

Heuristic stroke ordering: The synthetic stroke ordering relies on a simple depth-first search on spatial proximity. While stochastic skipping helps, real human drawing order often reflects semantic parts (e.g., drawing legs first, or backrest first) rather than purely spatial nearest-neighbor traversals.
Resolution bottlenecks: The 3D generation is constrained by the frozen 64^3 VQ-VAE latent space, which leads to visible oversmoothing of fine structural details and thin geometric features.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear limitation in prior VR sketch-to-3D shape literature: existing methods treat 3D sketches as unordered point clouds, ignoring stroke and point temporal connectivity.

The dataset contribution is substantial: VRSKETCH2SHAPE provides over 20,000 synthetic sketch-shape pairs and 900 carefully collected real VR sketches across four categories with stroke and point temporal order preserved, significantly improving upon prior single-category, unaligned benchmarks.

The proposed architecture is well-grounded: coupling an order-aware BERT-style sketch encoder (using continuous Fourier position embeddings for both spatial coordinates and sequence indices) with a latent diffusion model (SDFusion) yields large quantitative gains over existing point-based and multi-view baselines (e.g., Luo et al. and LAS-Diffusion).

The experimental validation is thorough, including zero-shot and few-shot synthetic-to-real transfer, user studies on free-hand sketches, partial sketch completion, and analysis on sampling speed/steps and sketcher expertise.
weaknesses: The title and main framing emphasize 'Order Matters' as capturing human drawing intent, but the ablation in Appendix A-1 reveals that reversing stroke order has virtually no effect and DFS vs. BFS traversal is simply an inductive bias. The performance sensitivity primarily stems from point connectivity and sequential token structuring rather than true temporal human sketch chronology.
The geometric resolution is constrained by the frozen 64^3 3D VQ-VAE, leading to noticeably smooth, low-frequency geometric reconstructions that struggle to capture thin structures or sharp edges.

The dataset and evaluation are restricted to four rigid object classes (chairs, tables, cabinets, airplanes); tests on unseen classes (Figure A-5) indicate noticeable collapse toward the dominant furniture priors.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated premise: treating 3D VR sketches as structured, temporally ordered stroke sequences rather than discarding connectivity and sequence information by treating them as unordered point clouds (PointNet-style) or 2D projections.

Valuable dataset contribution: introduces a scalable, training-free synthetic VR sketch generation pipeline (20k+ pairs) alongside a high-quality real VR sketch benchmark (900 shapes across 4 categories) with preserved stroke/point order and surface snapping.

Well-designed technical architecture: adapts transformer/BERT sequence modeling to 3D sketching using continuous Fourier coordinate embeddings alongside hierarchical stroke- and point-level positional encodings, successfully interfaced with latent diffusion (SDFusion).

Thorough empirical evaluation: demonstrates significant quantitative improvements in Chamfer Distance and F-score over existing baselines (Luo et al. and LAS-diffusion) on both the established 3DVRChair dataset and the new benchmark. Includes insightful user studies and partial-sketch completion experiments.

Extensive ablation studies: carefully validates the importance of spatial Fourier encodings, stroke ordering, augmentations, and synthetic pre-training, as well as providing analysis on DDIM step speed-accuracy tradeoffs.
weaknesses: Nuance regarding the role of 'order': While the paper emphasizes temporal order, the ablation in Supplementary Tab. A-1 reveals that reversing stroke order (56.2 F-score vs. 56.8) and scrambling strokes (54.6) incur relatively mild drops, whereas scrambling point order has a larger impact. This suggests that local polyline continuity/connectivity is the dominant factor for full-sketch reconstruction, while temporal order primarily benefits partial/progressive sketch completion. The manuscript would benefit from clarifying this distinction in the main text.

Geometric resolution limits: Because the shape generator is built on top of a frozen 64^3 3D VQ-VAE latent space, the generated meshes exhibit visible oversmoothing and struggle to capture sharp geometric edges and delicate components.

Category breadth: The real sketch evaluation is limited to four rigid object categories (chairs, tables, cabinets, airplanes). While unseen class generalization is qualitatively inspected in the appendix, the diversity of annotated real shapes remains relatively modest.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and under-explored problem in 3D generative design: leveraging the sequential and temporal structure of 3D VR sketches rather than discarding it by treating sketches as unordered point clouds.

Provides a valuable benchmark and data generation pipeline: introduces an automated, learning-free synthetic stroke generation pipeline (20k+ pairs) alongside a carefully collected multi-category real VR sketch dataset (900 sketches with full temporal order and surface snapping across four classes).

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: demonstrates substantial quantitative improvements over competitive baselines (e.g., Luo et al. and LAS-Diffusion) on both the established 3DVRChair benchmark and the proposed multi-category benchmark.

Thorough experimental validation: includes an informative human user study on free-hand vs. reference-guided sketching, extensive component ablations (ordering, data augmentation, pre-training, input modalities), cross-modal shape completion experiments, and out-of-distribution class tests.
weaknesses: The central premise ('Order Matters') is somewhat nuanced by empirical findings: in Appendix Table A-1, reversing stroke order yields almost identical performance (56.2 vs. 56.8 F-score, with CD slightly improving from 5.1 to 5.0), and stroke scrambling causes only minor degradation. As the authors acknowledge, the benefit stems primarily from sequential connectivity and tokenization rather than fidelity to actual human chronological drawing sequence.

Technical novelty is somewhat modular and incremental: the framework couples a BERT-style transformer encoder using standard spatial/temporal Fourier encodings with an off-the-shelf latent diffusion model (SDFusion).

Geometric resolution is limited by the underlying frozen 3D VQ-VAE grid (64^3 SDF resolution), resulting in visibly smoothed/blobby shapes that lack sharp topological and fine-grained geometric features.

The dataset scope, while an improvement over existing single-category benchmarks, remains restricted to four rigid object categories (chairs, tables, cabinets, airplanes) with a relatively small real-sketch collection (900 samples).
